s: Nisus is the son of Hyrtacus (of noble blood)
q: His father Hyrtacus of noble blood;

s: Nisus is a friend of Euryalus (sharing one care, delight, and common hazard)
q: Beside him stood Euryalus, his friend: Euryalus, than whom the Trojan host No fairer face, or sweeter air, could boast. Scarce had the down to shade his cheeks begun. One was their care, and their delight was one: One common hazard in the war they shar’d, And now were both by choice upon the guard.

s: Nisus is skilled with bow and spear (especially with unerring shafts)
q: Well could he bear His lance in fight, and dart the flying spear, But better skill’d unerring shafts to send.

s: Euryalus is a young Trojan warrior (not yet fully bearded)
q: Euryalus, than whom the Trojan host No fairer face, or sweeter air, could boast. Scarce had the down to shade his cheeks begun.

s: Euryalus is a friend of Nisus (bound by shared danger and glory)
q: Beside him stood Euryalus, his friend:

s: Euryalus is the son of Euryalus’s mother (his mother is of Priam’s royal race)
q: Of Priam’s royal race my mother came— And sure the best that ever bore the name— Whom neither Troy nor Sicily could hold From me departing, but, o’erspent and old, My fate she follow’d.

s: Ascanius orders the more experienc’d
q: Ascanius bids ’em be conducted in, Ord’ring the more experienc’d to begin.

s: Ascanius promises Ascanius’s gifts (to Nisus and Euryalus for their mission)
q: Your common gift shall two large goblets be Of silver, wrought with curious imagery, And high emboss’d, which, when old Priam reign’d, My conqu’ring sire at sack’d Arisba gain’d; And more, two tripods cast in antique mould, With two great talents of the finest gold; Beside a costly bowl, ingrav’d with art, Which Dido gave, when first she gave her heart.

s: Mnestheus’s lion’s hide is given to Euryalus (for bodily defense)
q: Great Mnestheus gave his friend A lion’s hide, his body to defend;

s: Turnus cares for my ships (peculiar)
q: Trojan race, your needless aid forbear, And know, my ships are my peculiar care

s: Nisus and Euryalus’s mission is a attempt to reach Aeneas (through a passage near the sea)
q: Betwixt two paths, which at the gate divide, Close by the sea, a passage we have spied, Which will our way to great Aeneas guide.

s: war is a conflict between Trojans and Rutulians (around the Trojan camp)
q: The Trojans view the dusty cloud from far, And the dark menace of the distant war.

s: Turnus possesses Turnus’s horse (a piebald steed of Thracian strain)
q: The fiery Turnus flew before the rest: A piebald steed of Thracian strain he press’d;

s: Aeneas is absent from Trojan camp (while seeking the Arcadian prince)
q: Aeneas, gone to seek th’ Arcadian prince, Has left the Trojan camp without defence;

s: Aeneas raises Tuscans (in distant parts to provide succours)
q: And, short of succours there, employs his pains In parts remote to raise the Tuscan swains.

s: Iris appears as rainbow (in flight)
q: This said, on equal wings she pois’d her weight, And form’d a radiant rainbow in her flight.

s: Juno sends Iris (to find Turnus)
q: The various Iris Juno sends with haste, To find bold Turnus, who, with anxious thought, The secret shade of his great grandsire sought.

s: Euryalus beholds the girdle-belt (with nails of burnish’d gold)
q: Nor did his eyes less longingly behold The girdle-belt, with nails of burnish’d gold.

s: Euryalus possesses Euryalus's caparison (taken from Rhamnes's horse)
q: Yet, fond of gaudy spoils, the boy would stay To make the rich caparison his prey, Which on the steed of conquer’d Rhamnes lay.

s: Euryalus is pursued and captured in the pursuit and capture of Euryalus
q: The sound approach’d; and suddenly he view’d The foes inclosing, and his friend pursued, Forelaid and taken, while he strove in vain The shelter of the friendly shades to gain.

s: Volscens commands Volscens's three hundred horse (as their guide)
q: But far they had not pass’d, before they spied Three hundred horse, with Volscens for their guide.

s: Volscens possesses Volscens's sword (drawn in anger)
q: “But thou,” he cries, “Shalt pay for both,” and at the pris’ner flies With his drawn sword.

s: Volscens is killed by Nisus (in revenge for Euryalus)
q: Then whirl’d aloft his sword with all his might: Th’ unerring steel descended while he spoke, Pierc’d his wide mouth, and thro’ his weazon broke.

s: sleeping enemy host is a sleeping army (careless, drunk, and dispersed)
q: They found the careless host dispers’d upon the plain, Who, gorg’d, and drunk with wine, supinely snore.

s: Volscens's three hundred horse is guided by Volscens
q: But far they had not pass’d, before they spied Three hundred horse, with Volscens for their guide.

s: Volscens's three hundred horse is sent by the queen's legion (the swift horse accompanying the legion)
q: The queen a legion to King Turnus sent; But the swift horse the slower foot prevent,

s: Nisus is a friend of Euryalus
q: His only crime (if friendship can offend) Is too much love to his unhappy friend.”

s: the forest is a dense woodland (dark and difficult to traverse)
q: Black was the forest: thick with beech it stood, Horrid with fern, and intricate with thorn; Few paths of human feet, or tracks of beasts, were worn.

s: Messapus's helmet is worn by Euryalus (taken as spoils)
q: Messapus’ helm he finds among the rest, And laces on, and wears the waving crest.

s: the nocturnal raid shows his friend the sight
q: Observing Nisus shew’d his friend the sight: “Behold a conquest gain’d without a fight. Occasion offers, and I stand prepar’d;

s: the nocturnal raid targets sleeping enemy host (during the night)
q: They found the careless host dispers’d upon the plain, Who, gorg’d, and drunk with wine, supinely snore.

s: the slaughter of the sleeping soldiers includes Rhamnes's sleeping slaves
q: Him and his sleeping slaves he slew;

s: the pursuit and capture of Euryalus blocks all passages (to cross their way)
q: The speedy horse all passages belay, And spur their smoking steeds to cross their way,

s: friendship between Nisus and Euryalus is a deep friendship (mutually devoted)
q: His only crime (if friendship can offend) Is too much love to his unhappy friend.”

s: fame and immortality through poetry is granted to Nisus (through the poet’s verse)
q: O happy friends! for, if my verse can give Immortal life, your fame shall ever live,

s: Nisus participates in the nocturnal raid (with Euryalus)
q: Thus arm’d they went. The noble Trojans wait Their issuing forth, and follow to the gate

s: fame and immortality through poetry is granted to Euryalus (through the poet’s verse)
q: O happy friends! for, if my verse can give Immortal life, your fame shall ever live,

s: Fortune cannot prevent Rhamnes's death (despite his prophetic knowledge)
q: But fate by prescience cannot be remov’d.

s: Nisus possesses Nisus's spear
q: Resolv’d at length, his pointed spear he shook;

s: Nisus possesses Nisus's sword
q: Softly he spoke; then striding took his way, With his drawn sword, where haughty Rhamnes lay;

s: Nisus dies with Euryalus (after killing Volscens)
q: Then quiet on his bleeding bosom fell, Content, in death, to be reveng’d so well.

s: Euryalus is a friend of Nisus
q: His only crime (if friendship can offend) Is too much love to his unhappy friend.”

s: Turnus calls his troops (to fight)
q: When early Turnus, wak’ning with the light, All clad in armour, calls his troops to fight.

s: Volscians uses siege equipment (including ladders and a shield shed)
q: These fill the ditch; those pull the bulwarks down: Some raise the ladders; others scale the town.

s: Euryalus’s mother loves Euryalus
q: Thus, then, my lov’d Euryalus appears! Thus looks the prop of my declining years!

s: Euryalus’s mother is related to Euryalus (as his mother)
q: Soon hasty fame thro’ the sad city bears The mournful message to the mother’s ears.

s: Euryalus’s mother weaves a mantle (for Euryalus)
q: Or spread the mantle (made for other ends) On his dear body, which I wove with care,

s: Ascanius is ruled by Old Butes
q: Old Butes’ form he took, Anchises’ squire, Now left, to rule Ascanius, by his sire:

s: Ascanius is praised by Apollo (as offspring of gods and founder of the Julian line)
q: Advance, illustrious youth, increase in fame, And wide from east to west extend thy name; Offspring of gods thyself; and Rome shall owe To thee a race of demigods below.

s: Ascanius belongs to the Julian line (as its beginning)
q: This is the way to heav’n: the pow’rs divine From this beginning date the Julian line.

s: Ascanius uses the bow (in his first martial combat)
q: Then young Ascanius, who, before this day, Was wont in woods to shoot the savage prey, First bent in martial strife the twanging bow, And exercis’d against a human foe

s: Turnus calls his troops (to fight)
q: When early Turnus, wak’ning with the light, All clad in armour, calls his troops to fight.

s: Jupiter is a god (who hears Ascanius’s prayer)
q: Jove bow’d the heav’ns, and lent a gracious ear, And thunder’d on the left, amidst the clear.

s: Jupiter commands Iris (to remove Turnus from the Trojan camp)
q: For Jove, with sour commands, sent Iris down, To force th’ invader from the frighted town.

s: Apollo is a god (of archery)
q: The god of archers gives thy youth a part Of his own praise, nor envies equal art.

s: Apollo assumes Butes (to speak to Ascanius)
q: Old Butes’ form he took, Anchises’ squire, Now left, to rule Ascanius, by his sire:

s: Pandarus beholds his brother
q: When Pandarus beheld his brother kill’d, The town with fear and wild confusion fill’d,

s: Pandarus is related to Bitias (as his brother)
q: When Pandarus beheld his brother kill’d, The town with fear and wild confusion fill’d,

s: Pandarus is the guardian of the gate (which he opens and closes)
q: He turns the hinges of the heavy gate With both his hands, and adds his shoulders to the weight

s: Bitias is related to Pandarus (as his brother)
q: When Pandarus beheld his brother kill’d,

s: Turnus possesses martial ardour (which he inspires in his soldiers)
q: His martial men with fierce harangue he fir’d, And his own ardour in their souls inspir’d.

s: Numanus is killed by Ascanius (with an arrow)
q: Sounded at once the bow; and swiftly flies The feather’d death, and hisses thro’ the skies. The steel thro’ both his temples forc’d the way: Extended on the ground, Numanus lay.

s: the Trojan walls is a fortification (defended by the Trojans)
q: They line their trenches, and they man their walls.

s: war is a armed conflict (between the Trojans and Italians)
q: And the vast circuit of the fatal war;

s: the Trojans mans their walls
q: Meantime the Trojans run, where danger calls; They line their trenches, and they man their walls.

s: the Trojans practices defensive fighting (as veterans of the siege of Troy)
q: Taught, by their ten years’ siege, defensive fight,

s: the Trojans occupies the Trojan walls (in defense of the camp)
q: Meantime the Trojans run, where danger calls; They line their trenches, and they man their walls.

s: Volscians is a attacking army (assaulting the Trojan walls)
q: The Volscians bear their shields upon their head, And, rushing forward, form a moving shed.

s: Jupiter is a god (supreme deity)
q: Then thus th’ almighty sire began: “Ye gods,

s: Venus possesses Cythera (sacred island domain)
q: Mine is Cythera, mine the Cyprian tow’rs:

s: Juno is a goddess (queen of heaven)
q: But is my crime—the Queen of Heav’n offends, If she presume to save her suff’ring friends!

s: Juno supports her suff’ring friends
q: If she presume to save her suff’ring friends!

s: Aeneas is a Trojan (leader and hero)
q: Meantime the hero cuts the nightly tide:

s: Aeneas leads the Trojans (in the war for Latium)
q: Aeneas leads; upon his stern appear Two lions carv’d, which rising Ida bear

s: Aeneas possesses shield of Aeneas (divinely made and impenetrable)
q: Thyself the fated sword of Vulcan wield, And bear aloft th’ impenetrable shield.

s: Aeneas wields sword of Vulcan (fated weapon)
q: Thyself the fated sword of Vulcan wield, And bear aloft th’ impenetrable shield.

s: Aeneas travels to Tyrrhene coast (to seek military aid)
q: For, anxious, from Evander when he went, He sought the Tyrrhene camp, and Tarchon’s tent;

s: Turnus is a King
q: King Turnus wonder’d at the fight renew’d,

s: Jupiter presides over council of the gods (as sovereign)
q: Jupiter, calling a council of the gods, forbids them to engage in either party.

s: Turnus leads Rutulians (in battle)
q: Now Turnus leads his troops without delay, Advancing to the margin of the sea.

s: Mezentius prepares vengeance (proud)
q: What vengeance proud Mezentius had prepar’d:

s: Lausus is a youth (pious and virtuous)
q: Mezentius is described as an atheist; Lausus as a pious and virtuous youth.

s: Pallas is fixed to his side (young)
q: His left young Pallas kept, fix’d to his side,

s: Ascanius is pressed by your insulting foes (in his camp distress’d)
q: But young Ascanius, in his camp distress’d, By your insulting foes is hardly press’d.

s: Ascanius is son of Aeneas (divine sonship asserted by Venus)
q: The father may be cast on coasts unknown, Struggling with fate; but let me save the son.

s: Tarchon joins the Trojan troops (the Tuscan)
q: Tarchon, without delay, the treaty signs, And to the Trojan troops the Tuscan joins.

s: Tarchon joins the Trojans (as military ally)
q: Tarchon, without delay, the treaty signs, And to the Trojan troops the Tuscan joins.

s: Jupiter commands the gods (to remain neutral in the war)
q: The war henceforward be resign’d to fate: Each to his proper fortune stand or fall; Equal and unconcern’d I look on all.

s: the Trojans are from Troy (exiled people)
q: By ruin’d Troy, yet smoking from the flame,

s: the Trojans are allied with Tuscans (in relief of their besieged camp)
q: And to the Trojan troops the Tuscan joins.

s: Rutulians are led by Turnus (in the war for Latium)
q: Now Turnus leads his troops without delay,

s: Tuscans is a army (foreign force allied with Aeneas)
q: The Tuscan leaders, and their army sing, Which follow’d great Aeneas to the war:

s: Latium is a land (Latian territory contested in war)
q: Why this protracted war, when my commands Pronounc’d a peace, and gave the Latian lands?

s: Troy is ruined ruin’d (yet smoking from the flame)
q: By ruin’d Troy, yet smoking from the flame,

s: Ida is dear to wand’ring Trojans (ever)
q: Ida, to wand’ring Trojans ever dear.

s: war is a war (conflict between Trojans and Latins)
q: Why this protracted war, when my commands Pronounc’d a peace, and gave the Latian lands?

s: Jupiter is father of Venus (divine parentage)
q: And I, thy daughter, wait another wound.

s: Turnus’s assault on the Trojan camp is a siege (conducted by the enemy)
q: Meantime, intent upon their siege, the foes Within their walls the Trojan host inclose:

s: Trojan fleet is a fleet (fleet that carries Aeneas and his allies)
q: Full thirty ships transport the chosen train For Troy’s relief, and scour the briny main.

s: Fortune determines warfare (ultimate outcome of each side)
q: The war henceforward be resign’d to fate: Each to his proper fortune stand or fall;

s: Fortune finds their way
q: The Fates will find their way.”

s: divine intervention affects warfare (through gods and supernatural agents)
q: What fear or hope on either part divides Our heav’ns, and arms our powers on diff’rent sides?

s: Mother of the Gods transforms Trojan fleet (into immortal sea nymphs)
q: The mighty Mother chang’d our forms to these, And gave us life immortal in the seas.

s: Jupiter is husband of Juno (marital relationship)
q: An act that well became the wife of Jove!

s: council of the gods is a council (divine assembly)
q: Jupiter, calling a council of the gods, forbids them to engage in either party.

s: the gods participate in council debate (with divided sympathies)
q: Thus Juno. Murmurs rise, with mix’d applause, Just as they favour or dislike the cause.

s: Venus protects Ascanius (as a mother and divine guardian)
q: Then, father, (if I still may use that name,) By ruin’d Troy, yet smoking from the flame, I beg you, let Ascanius, by my care, Be freed from danger, and dismiss’d the war:

s: Pallas is a Arcadian prince
q: Pallas, who with disdain and grief had view’d His foes pursuing, and his friends pursued,

s: Turnus addresses single fight (on foot)
q: Then Turnus, from his chariot leaping light, Address’d himself on foot to single fight.

s: Turnus is a chief (deserting)
q: What will they say of their deserting chief The war was mine: I fly from their relief;

s: Turnus is descended from Pilumnus (in the fourth degree)
q: And, in the fourth degree, from god Pilumnus came;

s: Turnus is protected by Juno (through divine intervention)
q: But Juno, mov’d with pity, both withstood. And thrice repress’d his rage; strong gales supplied,

s: Turnus’s flight by ship is landed at his native shores
q: At length she lands him on his native shores, And to his father’s longing arms restores.

s: Aeneas is a Trojan hero (leading the Trojan forces)
q: With strength like his, the Trojan hero stood; And soon the fields with falling corps were strow’d,

s: Aeneas is father of Ascanius
q: By young Iulus, by thy father’s shade,

s: Aeneas is an enemy of Turnus (in the Italian war)
q: Meantime Aeneas seeks his absent foe, And sends his slaughter’d troops to shades below.

s: Lausus is a warrior (a prominent participant in the war)
q: But Lausus, no small portion of the war,

s: Pallas is son of Evander
q: By my great sire, by his establish’d name, And early promise of my future fame;

s: Evander is father of Pallas
q: By my great sire, by his establish’d name, And early promise of my future fame;

s: Evander receives praises (at once restor’d)
q: O grace and grief of war! at once restor’d, With praises, to thy sire, at once deplor’d!

s: Juno is a goddess (queen of the gods and wife of Jupiter)
q: Meantime the King of Gods and Mortal Man Held conference with his queen, and thus began:

s: Juno is wife of Jupiter (and his sister goddess)
q: My sister goddess, and well-pleasing wife,

s: Juno supports Turnus (seeking to preserve him from immediate death)
q: Now speedy death attends the guiltless youth, If my presaging soul divines with truth; Which, O! I wish, might err thro’ causeless fears, And you (for you have pow’r) prolong his years!”

s: Jupiter is a king of gods and mortal men
q: Meantime the King of Gods and Mortal Man Held conference with his queen, and thus began:

s: Jupiter is father of Sarpedon (a mortal son who dies in battle)
q: My own Sarpedon fell beneath his foe; Nor I, his mighty sire, could ward the blow.

s: Jupiter permits Turnus’s flight by ship (as a temporary reprieve from immediate fate)
q: Since in my pow’r and goodness you confide, If for a little space, a lengthen’d span, You beg reprieve for this expiring man, I grant you leave to take your Turnus hence From instant fate, and can so far dispense.

s: Arcadians are allies of Pallas (in battle against the Latins)
q: Now, to renew the charge, th’ Arcadians came: Sight of such acts, and sense of honest shame, And grief, with anger mix’d, their minds inflame.

s: Pallas leads Arcadians (in battle)
q: So Pallas’ troops their scatter’d strength unite, And, pouring on their foes, their prince delight.

s: Arcadians bears the breathless body (from th’ unhappy field)
q: The sad Arcadians, from th’ unhappy field, Bear back the breathless body on a shield.

s: Trojan camp is besieged the camp (in vain)
q: At length Ascanius and the Trojan train Broke from the camp, so long besieg’d in vain.

s: war involves the Trojans (against the Italian peoples)
q: To the rude shock of war both armies came; Their leaders equal, and their strength the same.

s: Fate determines Pallas’s death (despite divine sympathy and intervention)
q: Both doom’d to fall, but fall by greater hands.

s: Fate determines Turnus’s death (though his immediate death is temporarily deferred)
q: Ev’n Turnus shortly shall resign his breath, And stands already on the verge of death.”

s: Tiber is a sacred stream (addressed by Pallas before throwing his spear)
q: O sacred stream, direct my flying dart, And give to pass the proud Halesus’ heart!

s: Hercules is guest of Evander (once on earth)
q: Alcides, once on earth Evander’s guest,

s: Hercules is invoked by Pallas (before his combat with Turnus)
q: Young Pallas, when he saw the chief advance Within due distance of his flying lance, Prepares to charge him first, resolv’d to try If fortune would his want of force supply; And thus to Heav’n and Hercules address’d:

s: Pallas is a young warrior (in his first fighting campaign)
q: One day first sent thee to the fighting field, Beheld whole heaps of foes in battle kill’d;

s: Camers is son of Volscens (and king of Amycla)
q: Camers was son to Volscens lately slain, In wealth surpassing all the Latian train, And in Amycla fix’d his silent easy reign.

s: Pallas’s belt is made by Eurytion (as an ornate golden belt)
q: Then snatch’d the shining belt, with gold inlaid; The belt Eurytion’s artful hands had made,

s: Aeneas is a Trojan (pious prince and hero)
q: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate, And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate, Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore.

s: Juno favors Carthage (more than Argos or Samos)
q: Carthage the name; belov’d by Juno more Than her own Argos, or the Samian shore.

s: Juno persecutes the Trojans (during their voyage)
q: For this, far distant from the Latian coast She drove the remnants of the Trojan host;

s: Juno commands Aeolus (to unleash the winds against the Trojans)
q: Raise all thy winds; with night involve the skies; Sink or disperse my fatal enemies.

s: Venus is the mother of Aeneas (divine mother)
q: Thou shalt behold thy wish’d Lavinian walls; And, ripe for heav’n, when fate Aeneas calls, Then shalt thou bear him up, sublime, to me:

s: Venus appeals to Jupiter (on behalf of Aeneas and the Trojans)
q: When Venus saw, she with a lowly look, Not free from tears, her heav’nly sire bespoke:

s: Jupiter is a god (Father of the Gods and King of Gods and Men)
q: To whom the Father of th’ immortal race, Smiling with that serene indulgent face, With which he drives the clouds and clears the skies,

s: Jupiter is the father of Venus (as her heavenly sire)
q: When Venus saw, she with a lowly look, Not free from tears, her heav’nly sire bespoke:

s: Jupiter fixes the fate of Aeneas (by an unalterable decree)
q: Daughter, dismiss thy fears; to thy desire The fates of thine are fix’d, and stand entire. Thou shalt behold thy wish’d Lavinian walls;

s: Aeneas is forced by Fate (to leave Troy)
q: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate, And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate, Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore.

s: Jupiter promises Rome (an immortal empire)
q: To them no bounds of empire I assign, Nor term of years to their immortal line.

s: Neptune is a god (ruler of the sea)
q: The realms of ocean and the fields of air Are mine, not his. By fatal lot to me The liquid empire fell, and trident of the sea.

s: Neptune calms the storm (by exercising authority over the sea)
q: He spoke; and, while he spoke, he smooth’d the sea, Dispell’d the darkness, and restor’d the day.

s: Aeolus is a ruler (of the winds and storms)
q: Where, in a spacious cave of living stone, The tyrant Aeolus, from his airy throne, With pow’r imperial curbs the struggling winds, And sounding tempests in dark prisons binds.

s: the Trojans is driven from the Latian coast (far distant)
q: For this, far distant from the Latian coast She drove the remnants of the Trojan host;

s: the Trojans wander for Aeneas’s voyage (seven years)
q: And sev’n long years th’ unhappy wand’ring train Were toss’d by storms, and scatter’d thro’ the main.

s: the Trojans are destined for Italy (under Jupiter’s decree)
q: Thro’ various hazards and events, we move To Latium and the realms foredoom’d by Jove.

s: the Trojans are received by Carthage (as protected guests)
q: The queen herself suspends the rigid laws, The Trojans pities, and protects their cause.

s: Carthage is a city (Tyrian colony in Africa)
q: Against the Tiber’s mouth, but far away, An ancient town was seated on the sea; A Tyrian colony; the people made Stout for the war, and studious of their trade: Carthage the name;

s: Aeneas is hated by Juno (with unrelenting hostility)
q: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate, And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate, Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore.

s: Carthage is favored by Juno (more than Argos and Samos)
q: Carthage the name; belov’d by Juno more Than her own Argos, or the Samian shore.

s: Carthage is destined to be destroyed by the Trojan race (according to ancient prophecy)
q: That times to come should see the Trojan race Her Carthage ruin, and her tow’rs deface;

s: Italy is the destination of the Trojans (their foreordained land)
q: A race of wand’ring slaves, abhorr’d by me, With prosp’rous passage cut the Tuscan sea; To fruitful Italy their course they steer,

s: Latium is the future realm of Aeneas (the promised land)
q: Thro’ various hazards and events, we move To Latium and the realms foredoom’d by Jove.

s: Rome is founded by Romulus (as a city of the Romans)
q: Then Romulus his grandsire’s throne shall gain, Of martial tow’rs the founder shall become, The people Romans call, the city Rome.

s: Rome rules Roman imperial rule (with universal dominion)
q: The subject world shall Rome’s dominion own, And, prostrate, shall adore the nation of the gown.

s: Roman imperial rule has no assigned limit years (by Jupiter’s decree)
q: To them no bounds of empire I assign, Nor term of years to their immortal line.

s: Troy is the origin of the Trojans (their former homeland)
q: Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore.

s: the storm controls the struggling winds (with pow’r imperial)
q: Thus rag’d the goddess; and, with fury fraught. The restless regions of the storms she sought, Where, in a spacious cave of living stone, The tyrant Aeolus, from his airy throne, With pow’r imperial curbs the struggling winds,

s: Aeneas is destined to rule Latium (after winning the war)
q: Long labours, both by sea and land, he bore, And in the doubtful war, before he won The Latian realm, and built the destin’d town;

s: the storm scatters Trojan fleet (across the sea)
q: The Trojans, after a seven years’ voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one, and scatters the rest.

s: Trojan fleet is scattered by the storm (with one ship sunk)
q: The Trojans, after a seven years’ voyage, set sail for Italy, but are overtaken by a dreadful storm, which Aeolus raises at the request of Juno. The tempest sinks one, and scatters the rest.

s: Trojan fleet has remaining ships seven (after the storm)
q: Sev’n ships within this happy harbour meet, The thin remainders of the scatter’d fleet.

s: the ships are sheltered by the harbor (after the storm)
q: Within a long recess there lies a bay: An island shades it from the rolling sea, And forms a port secure for ships to ride;

s: Mercury is sent by Jupiter (to secure a welcome for the Trojans)
q: He said, and sent Cyllenius with command To free the ports, and ope the Punic land To Trojan guests;

s: Dido rules Carthage (as queen)
q: The queen herself suspends the rigid laws, The Trojans pities, and protects their cause.

s: Dido protects the Trojans (as queen of Carthage)
q: The queen herself suspends the rigid laws, The Trojans pities, and protects their cause.

s: Romulus is a founder (of Rome)
q: Then Romulus his grandsire’s throne shall gain, Of martial tow’rs the founder shall become, The people Romans call, the city Rome.

s: Aeneas is ancestor of Rome (through the Trojan and Alban succession)
q: His banish’d gods restor’d to rites divine, And settled sure succession in his line, From whence the race of Alban fathers come, And the long glories of majestic Rome.

s: Remus sustains Romulus (with Quirinus)
q: And Remus with Quirinus shall sustain The righteous laws, and fraud and force restrain.

s: Julius Caesar is a ruler (of an empire bounded only by ocean and the heavens)
q: Then Caesar from the Julian stock shall rise, Whose empire ocean, and whose fame the skies Alone shall bound;

s: Aeneas is aided by Venus (as her son)
q: When Venus saw, she with a lowly look, Not free from tears, her heav’nly sire bespoke:

s: Aeneas is promised Italy (as his destined land)
q: Thou shalt behold thy wish’d Lavinian walls; And, ripe for heav’n, when fate Aeneas calls, Then shalt thou bear him up, sublime, to me:

s: Juno is a goddess (Queen of Heaven)
q: What goddess was provok’d, and whence her hate; For what offence the Queen of Heav’n began To persecute so brave, so just a man;

s: Juno is prayed to by nations
q: For length of years my fruitless force employ Against the thin remains of ruin’d Troy! What nations now to Juno’s pow’r will pray,

s: Aeneas possesses celestial shield (Vulcanian and highly resistant)
q: The Trojan chief, who, held at bay from far, On his Vulcanian orb sustain’d the war.

s: Aeneas is pious pious (as a defining disposition)
q: The pious Trojan then his jav’lin sent;

s: Aeneas kills Lausus (reluctantly, after Lausus refuses to withdraw)
q: For now the Fates prepar’d their sharpen’d shears; And lifted high the flaming sword appears, Which, full descending with a frightful sway, Thro’ shield and corslet forc’d th’ impetuous way, And buried deep in his fair bosom lay.

s: Aeneas kills Mezentius (in combat)
q: He said, and to the sword his throat applied. The crimson stream distain’d his arms around, And the disdainful soul came rushing thro’ the wound.

s: Lausus is a heroic youth (devoted to his father)
q: And here, heroic youth, ’tis here I must To thy immortal memory be just, And sing an act so noble and so new, Posterity will scarce believe ’tis true.

s: Lausus is the son of Mezentius
q: His father’s peril Lausus view’d with grief; He sigh’d, he wept, he ran to his relief.

s: Lausus protects Mezentius (by placing himself between Mezentius and Aeneas)
q: The pious youth, resolv’d on death, below The lifted sword springs forth to face the foe; Protects his parent, and prevents the blow.

s: Lausus wears his crest and armour (torn from his body)
q: His crest and armour, from his body torn, Thy shoulders, Lausus, and thy head adorn.

s: Lausus is killed by Aeneas (after defending Mezentius)
q: Which, full descending with a frightful sway, Thro’ shield and corslet forc’d th’ impetuous way, And buried deep in his fair bosom lay.

s: Lausus is mourned by Mezentius (as his beloved son)
q: What joys, alas! could this frail being give, That I have been so covetous to live? To see my son, and such a son, resign His life, a ransom for preserving mine!

s: Mezentius is a warrior (formidable and contemptuous)
q: He, like a solid rock by seas inclos’d, To raging winds and roaring waves oppos’d, From his proud summit looking down, disdains Their empty menace, and unmov’d remains.

s: Lausus’s death is a sacrifice (for preserving Mezentius)
q: To see my son, and such a son, resign His life, a ransom for preserving mine!

s: Rhoebus lives with me
q: O Rhoebus, we have liv’d too long for me— If life and long were terms that could agree!

s: Rhoebus is loyal to such a lord
q: For, after such a lord, I rest secure, Thou wilt no foreign reins, or Trojan load endure.”

s: the Trojan people fight Rutulians (in the battle)
q: From either host, the mingled shouts and cries Of Trojans and Rutulians rend the skies.

s: Rutulians fight the Trojan people (in the battle)
q: From either host, the mingled shouts and cries Of Trojans and Rutulians rend the skies.

s: battle is a equal contest (with alternating advances and retreats)
q: Thus equal deaths are dealt with equal chance; By turns they quit their ground, by turns advance: Victors and vanquish’d, in the various field, Nor wholly overcome, nor wholly yield.

s: battle is observed by the gods (from heaven)
q: The gods from heav’n survey the fatal strife, And mourn the miseries of human life.

s: Mezentius is the father of Lausus
q: His father’s peril Lausus view’d with grief; He sigh’d, he wept, he ran to his relief.

s: the gods observe battle (from heaven)
q: The gods from heav’n survey the fatal strife, And mourn the miseries of human life.

s: filial love motivates Lausus (to protect his father)
q: The pious youth, resolv’d on death, below The lifted sword springs forth to face the foe; Protects his parent, and prevents the blow.

s: filial love is expressed by Lausus (through self-sacrifice)
q: The pious youth, resolv’d on death, below The lifted sword springs forth to face the foe; Protects his parent, and prevents the blow.

s: Jupiter impels Mezentius (to arm and enter the fight)
q: Meantime, by Jove’s impulse, Mezentius arm’d,

s: Venus is concerned for Aeneas (during the battle)
q: Above the rest, two goddesses appear Concern’d for each: here Venus, Juno there.

s: Juno is concerned for Mezentius (during the battle)
q: Above the rest, two goddesses appear Concern’d for each: here Venus, Juno there.

s: Mezentius is chased from a throne (for foul misdeeds)
q: Chas’d from a throne, abandon’d, and exil’d For foul misdeeds, were punishments too mild:

s: Mezentius rides Rhoebus (his warhorse)
q: Yet, with a mind resolv’d, and unappall’d With pains or perils, for his courser call’d Well-mouth’d, well-manag’d, whom himself did dress With daily care, and mounted with success;

s: Mezentius is hated by Tuscans (as their king)
q: Against their king the Tuscan troops conspire; Such is their hate, and such their fierce desire Of wish’d revenge: on him, and him alone, All hands employ’d, and all their darts are thrown.

s: Mezentius is killed by Aeneas (in single combat)
q: He said, and to the sword his throat applied. The crimson stream distain’d his arms around, And the disdainful soul came rushing thro’ the wound.

s: Aeneas is a Trojan prince
q: The Trojan prince beheld him from afar, And dauntless undertook the doubtful war.

s: Aeneas is a pious chief
q: The pious chief, whom double cares attend For his unburied soldiers and his friend

s: Aeneas offers the peace with Troy (if Turnus yields or is defeated)
q: In equal arms let us alone contend; And let him vanquish, whom his fates befriend. This is the way (so tell him) to possess The royal virgin, and restore the peace

s: Turnus tries his cause in arms (to conquer or to die)
q: Turnus then should try His cause in arms, to conquer or to die

s: Turnus is accused of causing war (by Drances and the grieving Latins)
q: A broken league, a bride unjustly sought, A crown usurp’d, which with their blood is bought! These are the crimes with which they load the name Of Turnus, and on him alone exclaim

s: Turnus is supported by Amata (at the Latin court)
q: Nor Turnus wants a party, to support His cause and credit in the Latian court. His former acts secure his present fame, And the queen shades him with her mighty name

s: Turnus is opposed by Drances (as a long-standing enemy)
q: Drances, their chief, who harbour’d in his breast Long hate to Turnus, as his foe profess’d

s: Pallas is a son of Evander (young and newly dead)
q: The wretched father, ere his race is run, Shall view the fun’ral honours of his son

s: Pallas is a warrior (young and inexperienced in war)
q: That boiling blood would carry thee too far, Young as thou wert in dangers, raw to war

s: Pallas receives no dishonest wound
q: Thy Pallas no dishonest wound receiv’d.

s: Pallas is honored by Aeneas (with a solemn funeral procession)
q: And chose a thousand horse, the flow’r of all His warlike troops, to wait the funeral, To bear him back and share Evander’s grief

s: Aeneas is a victor
q: Yet first to Heav’n perform’d a victor’s vows:

s: Pallas is a friend of Ascanius (lamented after his death)
q: But what a champion has th’ Ausonian coast, And what a friend hast thou, Ascanius, lost

s: Evander is a father of Pallas (aged and grieving)
q: The wretched father, ere his race is run, Shall view the fun’ral honours of his son

s: Evander’s city is a Arcadian town
q: And now the fatal news by Fame is blown Thro’ the short circuit of th’ Arcadian town

s: Mezentius is a dead foe of Aeneas (the first major casualty of the war)
q: Fear is no more, for fierce Mezentius lies, As the first fruits of war, a sacrifice

s: Drances is a chief
q: Drances, their chief, who harbour’d in his breast Long hate to Turnus, as his foe profess’d

s: Aeneas erects the trophy (from Mezentius’s spoils)
q: He bar’d an ancient oak of all her boughs; Then on a rising ground the trunk he plac’d, Which with the spoils of his dead foe he grac’d

s: Latinus recognizes the Latian succession (as determined by fate and marriage to Lavinia)
q: Latinus, sunk in sorrow, finds too late, A foreign son is pointed out by fate; And, till Aeneas shall Lavinia wed, The wrath of Heav’n is hov’ring o’er his head

s: Lavinia is a royal virgin (whose marriage is disputed)
q: This is the way (so tell him) to possess The royal virgin, and restore the peace

s: Amata supports Turnus (with influence at the Latin court)
q: His former acts secure his present fame, And the queen shades him with her mighty name

s: Diomedes refuses the embassy to Diomedes (declining aid despite gifts and prayers)
q: That Diomedes refus’d his aid in war, Unmov’d with presents, and as deaf to pray’r

s: the Trojans participate in Pallas’s funeral procession (alongside Arcadian horse)
q: Thus while the Trojan and Arcadian horse To Pallantean tow’rs direct their course, In long procession rank’d

s: Arcadians participate in Pallas’s funeral procession (escorting their dead prince)
q: Thus while the Trojan and Arcadian horse To Pallantean tow’rs direct their course, In long procession rank’d

s: Latins perform funeral rites (for their dead after the truce)
q: The conquer’d Latians, with like pious care, Piles without number for their dead prepare

s: the dead deserve common rites (when they die in fair battle)
q: They plead, that none those common rites deny To conquer’d foes that in fair battle die

s: funeral rites are due to the dead (as a common obligation after battle)
q: They plead, that none those common rites deny To conquer’d foes that in fair battle die

s: the truce lasts twelve days (for preparation of funeral pyres)
q: Twelve days the term allow’d: and, during those, Latians and Trojans, now no longer foes, Mix’d in the woods, for fun’ral piles prepare

s: the trophy is dedicated to the God of War (as a war trophy)
q: A trophy sacred to the God of War.

s: the funeral of Pallas displays the spoils of foes (in long array by the hearse)
q: Besides, the spoils of foes in battle slain, When he descended on the Latian plain; Arms, trappings, horses, by the hearse are led In long array—th’ achievements of the dead

s: Pallas’s funeral procession includes Pallas’s horse Aethon (led behind the chariot)
q: To close the pomp, Aethon, the steed of state, Is led, the fun’rals of his lord to wait

s: the gods supports the juster side
q: The gods, he saw, espous’d the juster side, When late their titles in the field were tried

s: Fortune denies Pallas (a safe return to Evander)
q: She came; but brought not thee along, to bless My longing eyes, and share in my success: She grudg’d thy safe return, the triumphs due To prosp’rous valour, in the public view

s: Aeneas claims Latium (as allotted by fate)
q: I came not hither but by Heav’n’s command, And sent by fate to share the Latian land

s: Aeneas disputes Turnus (over Lavinia and the right to rule)
q: My right and his are in dispute: the slain Fell without fault, our quarrel to maintain

s: Aeneas sends Pallas’s body (to Evander’s city with funeral honors)
q: But first the corpse of our unhappy friend To the sad city of Evander send, Who, not inglorious, in his age’s bloom, Was hurried hence by too severe a doom

s: Aeneas grants the truce (for burying the dead)
q: Their suit, which was too just to be denied, The hero grants, and farther thus replied

s: Latian senate is a council of the Latins
q: The Latian senate to the council hall.

s: Diomede refuses Latin-Trojan peace proposal (and advises a truce)
q: He said no more; but, with this cold excuse, Refus’d th’ alliance, and advis’d a truce.”

s: the Greeks comes to destroy Troy
q: Of Grecians, who to Troy’s destruction came,

s: Troy is razed by the royal hand
q: The royal hand that raz’d unhappy Troy.

s: the Trojans makes the long defence
q: The long defence the Trojan people made,

s: Hector is a brave (equal in command)
q: The war protracted, and the siege delay’d, Were due to Hector’s and this hero’s hand: Both brave alike, and equal in command;
